title: Inside India's bold plan to transform its largest slum, Dharavi, into a multibillion-dollar development
summary: India's largest slum is being cleared to make room for a modern urban development to include rehabilitated slum housing plus luxury condos and office towers. It's a massive regeneration project,…

image.caption: An animation gif shows daily life in Dharavi, Mumbai, India's largest slum, where roughly a million people live in impoverished conditions. (Kate Kyle/CBC)

blocks.text: In a memorable flashback from the 2008 Oscar-winning film Slumdog Millionaire, brothers Jamal and Salim Malik sit atop an unfinished high-rise overlooking the Mumbai neighbourhood where they grew up. Their childhood slum has been bulldozed and replaced by luxury apartments and commercial skyscrapers.
"That used to be our slum. Can you believe that, huh?" Salim remarks. "Now, it's all business. India is at the centre of the world."

What was fiction on screen is now unfolding in reality. Frontend loaders have moved into parts of Dharavi, India’s largest slum and the second-largest in the world, and are looking to turn it into a billion-dollar development, launching one of Asia’s most ambitious urban redevelopment projects.

Shopkeeper Pooja Tiwari, 29, watches anxiously as the diggers encroach on her tiny shop. She’s eked out a meagre living here for 14 years, but her landlord announced she’d have to be out within a week.
"I am very scared because my income has depended on this shop for so many years," she said. "I don’t know what I’m going to do."
Pooja Tiwari loses her shop in the first demolitions of Mumbai's Dhavari slum. It's her only income and she's nervous about how she'll survive. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
'A better place to live'

Dharavi is home to an estimated one million people, sprawling across nearly 600 acres in the heart of Mumbai. From the air, it looks like a sea of thousands of bright blue tarps covering ramshackle, one- to three-storey structures.
At the heart of it is a dense rabbit warren of tiny rooms and lanes less than a metre wide, squished so tightly together that little sunlight reaches the ground, even at midday.
Households lack formal water and sewer systems, sharing communal taps and toilets, while tangled, outdated wiring supplies electricity.
Mumbai wants this slum gone. Where will 1 million people go?

Mahendra Kalyankar, CEO of the state's Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA), says that more than 1,000 people often share a single toilet, and 100 rely on one drinking water tap; the school dropout rate, he says, hovers around 40 per cent.
"New Dharavi will be a better place to live," he said, referring to the plans for modern tiny apartments in highrise buildings, with proper sanitation and hygiene.
State and city officials have tried for decades to uproot Dharavi. But this time a bold new plan is underway.

blocks.text: To transform the slum, the Maharashtra state government has partnered with the Adani Group, led by multi-billionaire Gautam Adani, in a public-private venture. Pranav Adani, the founder's nephew, described the conditions inside Dharavi as "inhuman," at a recent Mumbai conference, framing the project as building "a city in a city" and a huge opportunity.

Mahendra Kalyankar, CEO of the state Slum Rehabilitation Authority promises better living conditions for slum residents in Dharavi. With the Adani Group, the government is launching a big bold plan to build modern apartments alongside a glittering new residential and commercial centre in India's financial capital. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
Kalyankar says the difference this time is the injection of private capital, and the inclusion of the Adani Group, which can pay the substantial upfront costs.
"This project will be potentially successful when you infuse a lot of capital. That is the major issue," said Kalyankar.

It's valuable, because its sits on prime real estate next to the Bandra Kurla Complex, a landmark business district that houses banks, the stock exchange and multinational corporations. Local activists compare the 600-acre parcel to the Koh-i-Noor, the world-famous Indian diamond, just waiting to be claimed for a wealthy development.

"They are finding a big opportunity to extend this land to make BKC 2 and to make all the profit for one person [Adani] who is a big businessman of this city," said Samya Korde, a 26-year-old community organizer in Dharavi.
"Nobody dreams of living in choked lanes where sunlight doesn't come," she said. "So we want development to take place," but not by pushing residents out.
Many risk being pushed out

For over a year, surveyors have navigated Dharavi’s narrow alleys, measuring homes as small as 50 square feet and demanding paperwork to prove residency. Only families who can prove they lived in a street-level home there before 2000 are guaranteed a free apartment onsite.
Everyone else faces relocation: Some will be offered housing elsewhere, at a deep discount, while those who arrived more recently will be moved to rental units outside the area.

Samya Korde, 26, worries the plan to redevelop the Dharavi slum will mean a majority of its residents will be pushed out to other undesirable land, to make way for a wealthy urban neighbourhood. (Susan Ormiston/CBC)

Korde warns that 70 to 80 per cent of residents risk being labelled ineligible and pushed out to less desirable land. That figure is disputed, with the state government saying the surveys are incomplete. But critics and independent analysis argue that under the rules, a clear majority will not get new units on the same land.

She questions the development's motives: "There is one quote in Hindi: whether they want to remove poverty or whether they want to remove [the] poor," she said, "so that should be the aim — to transform people's lives and not to displace their homes."

blocks.text: To win over skeptics, the Adani Group recently opened an "Experience Centre" modelled after a luxury condo presentation facility. Visitors walk past murals celebrating Dharavi’s traditional artisans into a semi-circular theater playing a slick, IMAX-style promotional film.

The tour features a massive scale model of the future development — sleek commercial towers flanked by slum-rehabilitation high-rises — and a 350-square-foot show suite complete with a galley kitchen, a private toilet and two living spaces.

CBC News takes a tour of the Dharavi Experience Centre built by Adani to highlight the future look of the Dharavi Development. Luxury residences and office towers will be built alongside modern apartments for some slum residents. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
A lack of trust
For many residents, the glossy pitch masks a deep trust deficit.

Dharavi is an economic powerhouse. Generations of residents have built thriving, informal industries — leather tanneries, plastic recycling, commercial potteries — estimated to generate a billion dollars in annual turnover. Tradespeople remain skeptical of government promises that industrial operations can simply be moved into high-rise work zones serviced by freight elevators.

Meanwhile, an entrenched underground economy — including slum landlords profiting off unauthorized shanties and a local drug trade — is actively resisting a plan that allocates strictly one apartment per family.

For ordinary residents, the stakes are deeply personal. During a torrential downpour that threatened to flood the alleys and some of the homes, resident Khan Kabir Akhtar stood in a single-room home with his elderly grandfather, sitting on the bed.
Teenager Khan Kabir Akhtar and his grandfather both live in Dhavari. They want improvements, but in spite of harsh conditions, they don't want to move. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"My parents, my great-grandparents, [were] born here, so we want to live here," said Akhtar.

"We have to make it better, obviously," Akhtar admitted, but not at the cost of dislocating families. He doubts he will secure one of the new on-site apartments, and can't afford Mumbai market rates for another place to live.

blocks.text: Nearby, on what used to be railway lands, jackhammers are already pulverizing concrete and bulldozers are tearing into structures.

Down the lane, resident Rubina Sharif watches with cautious hope. Her modest home is slated for demolition, she’s waiting for interim housing before moving into a promised high-rise unit, given to qualifying slum residents.

"Redevelopment is a good plan," she said. "If it is genuinely meant to help the poor, then I am very happy about it. My expectation is simple: if we co-operate with them, they should also co-operate with us and not think only about themselves."

Rubina Sharif's home will be demolished. She welcomes improvements and is promised a new small apartment in Dharavi, but she worries about the developers making good on their commitments to the slum residents. (Saraskanth TK/CBC)

While the first new buildings could be ready within two years, the full transformation may take up to a decade. If successful, Mumbai’s massive urban experiment could serve as a blueprint for rapidly growing cities across Asia and Africa.

Yet in a city where affordable housing remains severely scarce and new slums can sprout within a month, erasing Dharavi will not solve Mumbai's housing crisis. While some families will finally trade squalor for modern living, hundreds of thousands of others face the prospect of being uprooted — and sequestered out of sight once again.
